questions.q: The story was published in 1955, a decade after Independence. Explain how the Nayi Kahani (New Story) movement's concerns—middle-class anxiety, urban alienation, the crisis of individual identity—might surface in a story about a young man trying to write his first story.
questions.a: Nayi Kahani shifted focus from village idealism (Premchand) to urban, educated protagonists grappling with thwarted aspirations and fragmented selves. A protagonist staring at a blank page with a single ink bottle embodies the new middle class's precarious creative agency—limited resources, self-doubt, and the pressure to produce something "meaningful" in a society redefining itself. A wrong answer that only mentions "post-Independence mood" without linking to specific movement traits (interiority, anti-hero, open endings) shows superficial historical awareness.

questions.q: The title centers on "<kbZ lky" (small ink bottle). In the context of a writer's first attempt, what does this object literally enable and what does it metaphorically represent? Give one literal and one metaphorical function.
questions.a: Literally: the ink bottle is the only writing material the narrator possesses, physically permitting the act of writing. Metaphorically: it represents the finite, precious reservoir of creative courage—the fear that one "mistake" (wasted ink) could end the attempt before it begins. A wrong answer treating it as mere setting detail misses the central conceit: the story is about scarcity as a creative condition, not just a plot device.
